newsitem.title: MEXICO: U.S. rate hike would spare LatAm -- Dornbusch.
newsitem.headline: U.S. rate hike would spare LatAm -- Dornbusch.

text.p: A hike in U.S. interest rates of 50 or 75 basis points would not harm flows of capital into Latin America, Massachusetts Institute of Technology economist Rudiger Dornbusch said at a conference on Wednesday.
"It will keep coming, perhaps more into equities and less into fixed income. Maybe to local currencies, but in total the money will keep coming," he said.
Markets in developing countries have grown faster than those in industrialized nations, while private investment flows have grown, analysts at the conference noted.
That has boosted flows of capital, but tightening global liquidity could affect those flows, particularly into Mexico, one analyst said.

"Institutional investors have dumped a lot of money into Mexico, but it is not necessarily well-informed investors. Basically they are investing in rates," said Joaquin Avila, managing director of Santander Investment.
He said those flows could weaken and that overall capital flows to Mexico could suffer if the nation is hit by another economic shock.
"If there is a shock Mexico will be severely affected," he said.
Dornbusch said that after the devaluation of the Mexican peso and its recent real appreciation the peso is at a similar level to where it was in 1992-1993.
He said that if the peso remains at its present level for another six months, then Mexico will be in a "precarious" situation.
In that situation, interest rates will rise, bad loans will increase and therre will be another currency crisis, he said.
While the central bank may believe that curbing inflation is the main problem, he said a lack of growth was an equally pressing concern for Mexico.
He said he thought the central bank had decided to allow the Mexican currency to gently depreciate.
